title: Unit final: heaps and top-K
sub: New problems, a k-th largest trace with duplicates, a threshold trap and explaining out loud
cards/0/q: New problems. Match each statement with its technique.
cards/0/pairs/0/0: After each number of a stream, return the k-th largest (#703)
cards/0/pairs/0/1: A min-heap of k, the answer is the root
cards/0/pairs/1/0: The k pairs with the smallest sums from two sorted arrays (#373)
cards/0/pairs/1/1: A heap of heads: after (i, j) comes (i, j + 1)
cards/0/pairs/2/0: Rearrange the characters of a string by descending frequency (#451)
cards/0/pairs/3/0: The k numbers closest to x in an unsorted array
cards/0/pairs/3/1: A max-heap of k by |a − x|
cards/0/pairs/4/0: The median of a stream of integers from 0 to 100
cards/1/q: Kth Largest Element in a Stream (#703): the constructor gets k and an initial array, and the method Add(val) returns the k-th largest after each number. Up to 10⁴ Add calls. What do you store?
cards/1/options/0: A min-heap of k: while there are fewer than k elements — Enqueue, then — EnqueueDequeue; the answer is Peek
cards/1/options/1: A max-heap of all numbers: on each Add remove k elements and put them back
cards/1/options/2: A sorted List<int>: BinarySearch and Insert, the answer is an element from the end
cards/1/explain: It is a stream and “the k best” — signals 1 and 3. The root of a min-heap of k is both the threshold and the answer. Add is O(log k), and EnqueueDequeue returns a number below the threshold without touching the heap. Memory is O(k), however many numbers arrive. The initial array may be shorter than k — that is why it starts with a plain Enqueue.
cards/1/wrong/1: k removals and k insertions on every Add are O(k log n) per call and O(n) memory. A min-heap of k keeps the answer at the root.
cards/1/wrong/2: Insert shifts the tail — O(n) per call, and memory grows with the stream. You do not need to store everything: numbers below the threshold will never become the answer.
cards/2/q: Sticks of length [2, 4, 3]. Joining two sticks costs the sum of their lengths and produces one stick of that length. You must join everything into one at minimum cost; it is known that joining the two shortest is always optimal. Which structure?
cards/2/options/0: A min-heap: remove the two shortest, put their sum back — O(n log n)
cards/2/options/1: Sort once and join from left to right
cards/2/options/2: A max-heap, as in Last Stone Weight
cards/2/explain: This is signal 2 from the first lesson — the two minimums of a changing set, again and again, only minimums instead of maximums. 2 + 3 = 5 (cost 5), 4 + 5 = 9 (cost 9), 14 in total. The new stick goes back into the set, so a single sort is not enough.
cards/2/wrong/1: After a join the new stick lands in the middle of the order, and the sort goes stale. On [1, 1, 1, 1] left to right gives 2, 3, 4 — 9 in total, while the heap gives 2, 2, 4 — 8 in total.
cards/2/wrong/2: Stones are smashed two heaviest at a time. Here it pays to take the shortest — you need a min-heap.
cards/3/task: Step through the trace on [3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], k = 4 — the array has duplicates. The rig asks twice what the root will be after Dequeue.
cards/3/goal/asks/0/q: 4 has arrived: the heap holds 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, size 5 > k. Dequeue removes one of the twos. What will the root be?
cards/3/goal/asks/0/explain: There are two twos in the heap, and Dequeue removes one element. The second two stays and rises to the root: the heap is 2, 3, 3, 4. The heap keeps duplicates as separate elements — and that is right, since the k-th is counted in sorted order, not among distinct values.
cards/3/goal/asks/1/q: 6 has arrived: the heap holds 3, 4, 5, 5, 6. Dequeue removes 3. What will the root — and the answer — be?
cards/3/goal/asks/1/explain: What remains is 4, 5, 5, 6 — the four largest, root 4. In descending order the array is 6, 5, 5, 4, …: the two fives take two places, and the fourth largest is 4. If the heap collapsed equal values, the answer would shift.
cards/4/q: On nums = [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2 this code returns 4, while the correct answer is 5. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/4/explain: The code removes the root before it knows whether x gets in — that is how DequeueEnqueue behaves. The threshold is thrown out even when x is below it. On the last step the heap holds 5, 6 and 4 arrives: Dequeue removes 5, Enqueue adds 4 — that leaves 4, 6 and the answer 4. Add first, then remove the extra one (Count > k), or use EnqueueDequeue directly.
cards/5/q: Complexity of the unit’s solutions. Which statements are true? Select all.
cards/5/options/0: The k-th largest via a min-heap of k — O(n log k) time and O(k) memory
cards/5/options/1: Quickselect with a random pivot is O(n) even in the worst case
cards/5/options/2: Merge k Sorted Lists via a heap of heads — O(N log k), where N is the total number of nodes
cards/5/options/3: Top K Frequent with buckets — O(n) time, but a bucket array of length n + 1
cards/5/options/4: In a MedianFinder on two heaps, FindMedian costs O(log n)
cards/5/explain: A heap of k is n operations at O(log k). Quickselect with a random pivot is O(n) on average, and the worst case stays O(n²), just unlikely. A heap of heads: each of the N nodes enters and leaves once, and the heap never exceeds k. Buckets are O(n), and their number does not depend on the number of distinct values. FindMedian only looks at the roots — O(1); it is AddNum that costs O(log n).
cards/6/q: Unity 2022: an AI event scheduler. Each event has a firing time; every frame you must run all events with time ≤ now, and for equal times — in the order they were added. What do you choose?
cards/6/options/0: Your own MinHeap keyed by (time, seq), where seq is the insertion number: each frame pop while the root ≤ now
cards/6/options/2: A SortedSet<float> of times and a dictionary “time → event”
cards/6/options/3: A List<Event> sorted by time every frame
cards/6/explain: The task is “the minimum of a changing set, again and again” — a heap. Unity has no PriorityQueue, so it is your own heap from the first lesson. A heap does not preserve the order of equals, so the insertion number goes into the key: a tuple compares field by field, and no ties remain. Each frame — Peek and Pop while the root’s time ≤ now: O(log n) per event.
cards/6/wrong/1: PriorityQueue appeared in .NET 6; Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) does not have it. And it is not stable: two events with the same time come out in any order.
cards/6/wrong/2: A set collapses equal values: a second event with the same time is not added, Add returns false. And every insertion is a tree node on the managed heap.
cards/6/wrong/3: Sorting every frame is O(n log n) again and again, although only a couple of events change. A heap does O(log n) per event.
cards/7/q: K Closest Points, but the centre is an arbitrary point (px, py), and all coordinates are up to 10⁵ in absolute value. What do you change in the solution with the squared distance in int?
cards/7/options/0: Compute the square in long: the difference reaches 2·10⁵, the sum of squares up to 8·10¹⁰
cards/7/options/1: Nothing: the squared distance always fits in int
cards/7/options/2: Switch to Math.Sqrt and double to avoid overflow
cards/7/explain: dx = x − px reaches 2·10⁵, dx² = 4·10¹⁰, and with dy² it is 8·10¹⁰. That is almost 40 times int.MaxValue ≈ 2.1·10⁹ — you need long and a long priority. The square root is still unnecessary: it does not change the order.
cards/7/wrong/1: In #973 it fit because coordinates were up to 10⁴ and the centre was at zero: the square ≤ 2·10⁸. Here the difference range is twice as wide and the values are 10 times larger — the square is 400 times larger.
cards/7/wrong/2: The square root is monotonic and does not change the order — it only costs time. Overflow is cured by the type: a square in long is exact, while a square root would only add work and rounding.
cards/8/q: You are solving Kth Largest Element in a Stream out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/8/items/0: Clarify: k-th in sorted order or among distinct values, may the initial array be shorter than k, how many Add calls
cards/8/items/1: Naively: keep everything sorted — O(n) per insertion and O(n) memory
cards/8/items/2: Recognize the pattern: a stream and “the k best” — a min-heap of k, the root is the threshold and the answer
cards/8/items/3: Write the code: while Count < k — Enqueue, then — EnqueueDequeue; the answer is Peek
cards/8/items/4: Run k = 3, initial array [4, 5, 8, 2], then Add(3) and Add(5)
cards/8/items/5: Complexity: Add is O(log k), memory O(k)
cards/8/items/6: Unity: there is no PriorityQueue — your own heap with PushPop
cards/8/explain: The same script as in every lesson of the unit. The dry run: heap 4, 5, 8; Add(3) — 3 is below the threshold 4, the answer is 4; Add(5) — 5 pushes out 4, heap 5, 5, 8, the answer is 5. The question about a short initial array explains why the first elements go through Enqueue.
